h1: Rosemary Infused Olive Oil, and How to Make It Safely
excerpt: Rosemary infused olive oil is simple, fragrant and easy to make badly, because any fresh herb sealed in oil at room temperature carries the same risk as fresh garlic does. Here is the safe method and the dried-herb alternative.
keyTakeaway: Rosemary infused olive oil should be made in small batches, refrigerated immediately, strained of the sprigs, and used within about a week. Fresh herbs in oil at room temperature can support the same low-acid, airless conditions that make garlic in oil a botulism risk. Dried rosemary avoids that risk entirely.

inlineAlt: Rosemary sprigs steeping in olive oil inside a small glass jar
intro: Rosemary infused olive oil is one of the simplest things to flavour at home, and the same rule that governs garlic infused olive oil applies here: fresh plant material sealed in oil at room temperature is a food safety risk, not just a style choice.
The fix is the same too. Make it in a small batch, refrigerate it the moment it is made, and use it within about a week.

sections.heading: Why does the same safety rule apply to rosemary?

blocks.text: Any fresh, low-acid plant material sealed under oil creates an airless, low-acid environment, which is what Clostridium botulinum needs to grow and produce its toxin. This is the same mechanism behind the fridge rule for [garlic infused olive oil](/blog/garlic-infused-olive-oil-and-how-to-do-it-safely), and it applies to fresh rosemary in oil for the same reason, not a different one.
Nothing in the smell or taste of the oil would warn you if this had happened. The safe habit is to refrigerate any fresh herb oil regardless of how low the risk feels for a particular herb.

sections.heading: Fresh rosemary or dried — which is safer?

blocks.text: Dried rosemary is the shelf-stable option, because it carries almost no free moisture for bacteria to use, and oil infused with dried herbs alone can be kept at room temperature. Fresh rosemary carries moisture on the leaf and stem, which is exactly the condition that needs refrigeration and a short window.

sections.heading: How do you make it safely at home?

blocks.text: Wash and thoroughly dry two or three fresh rosemary sprigs, since any residual water shortens the oil's life further. Submerge them fully in 250ml of extra virgin olive oil in a clean glass jar, seal it, and refrigerate straight away rather than leaving it to steep on the counter.

items: Wash the rosemary and pat it completely dry.
Warm the oil gently with the sprigs for ten minutes on the lowest heat, or steep cold in the fridge from the start.
Transfer to a clean jar, seal, and refrigerate immediately.
Strain out the rosemary after two to three days once the flavour has developed.
Keep refrigerated and use within about a week; discard anything left after that.

sections.heading: Cold infusion or gentle warm infusion?

blocks.text: Cold infusion means the sprigs steep in the refrigerator from the start, giving a slower, more subtle rosemary note over two to three days. Warm infusion means holding the oil and rosemary over the lowest heat for about ten minutes before chilling, which draws out more flavour faster. Both still need the fridge and the same short window afterward.
Warm infusion is not the same as frying the rosemary — a bare shimmer, never a simmer, is enough. Overheating scorches the leaves and turns the flavour bitter.

sections.heading: What is rosemary infused olive oil actually good for?

blocks.text: Bread dipping, drizzled over roasted potatoes or vegetables, finishing a grilled dish, or brushed over focaccia before baking. Its flavour is closer to pine and resin than garlic's, and a little goes further than most cooks expect on the first try.
It pairs particularly well with dishes that also carry olive oil as the base fat, since the rosemary note layers onto a flavour the dish already has rather than fighting it.

A **rosemary and basil** flavour, made with dried botanicals and strained out rather than fresh sprigs, is already part of the [Arabian Village Infused Collection](/products) — the shelf-stable version of exactly this idea, for anyone who would rather skip the fridge window.

sections.heading: Can you use the same jar for other fresh herbs?

blocks.text: The same rule applies to any fresh herb infused in oil — thyme, basil, chilli or garlic all create the same low-acid, airless conditions once submerged. Treat every fresh-herb oil as a refrigerate-and-use-soon product, and treat only fully dried ingredients as safe to leave at room temperature.
Mixing fresh herbs with garlic in the same jar does not add extra risk beyond what garlic alone already carries, but it does not remove it either — the same fridge and short window still apply.

conclusion.heading: Is it worth making at home?

blocks.text: Yes, in small batches and with the fridge rule respected — it is one of the easiest ways to lift a plain oil, and the safe method costs nothing beyond a little patience. If the short window feels inconvenient, a dried-rosemary version or a commercially bottled infused oil, made under a controlled process, is the shelf-stable alternative.

faqs.q: Is fresh rosemary infused olive oil safe to leave on the counter?
faqs.a: No. Any fresh herb sealed in oil at room temperature can create low-acid, airless conditions that support Clostridium botulinum. Refrigerate it as soon as it is made.

faqs.q: How long does rosemary infused olive oil last?
faqs.a: About a week, refrigerated and strained. Dried rosemary infused oil, kept at room temperature out of light, lasts considerably longer.

faqs.q: Can I make rosemary infused olive oil with dried rosemary instead?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the safer, longer-lasting option, since dried herbs carry almost no moisture for bacteria to use.

faqs.q: Does warming the oil make rosemary infused oil unsafe?
faqs.a: A gentle ten-minute warm still needs the same fridge and short window afterward as a cold infusion. The heat speeds up flavour, not safety.

faqs.q: Should I strain the rosemary out before storing?
faqs.a: Yes. Straining out the sprigs after two to three days removes plant material that could otherwise continue supporting bacterial growth in storage.

faqs.q: Is rosemary infused olive oil as risky as garlic infused olive oil?
faqs.a: The same underlying mechanism applies to both, so the same precautions apply: refrigerate immediately, strain, and use within about a week rather than treating either as shelf-stable.
